# Devanagari Script: Vowels & Consonants

Devanagari is a left-to-right abugida: each consonant carries an inherent "a" vowel unless modified. Hindi uses 11 vowels (svar) and 33 base consonants (vyanjan), arranged by place of articulation.

## Core Vocabulary

| Devanagari | Romanization | English |
|------------|--------------|---------|
| अ | a | inherent vowel "a" |
| आ | ā | long "aa" |
| इ | i | short "i" |
| ई | ī | long "ii" |
| उ | u | short "u" |
| ऊ | ū | long "uu" |
| ए | e | "e" as in "say" |
| ऐ | ai | "ai" |
| ओ | o | "o" as in "go" |
| औ | au | "au" |
| क | ka | velar "k" |
| ख | kha | aspirated "kh" |
| ग | ga | "g" |
| च | ca | "ch" as in "church" |
| ज | ja | "j" |
| ट | ṭa | retroflex "t" |
| त | ta | dental "t" |
| द | da | dental "d" |
| न | na | "n" |
| प | pa | "p" |
| ब | ba | "b" |
| म | ma | "m" |
| य | ya | "y" |
| र | ra | "r" |
| ल | la | "l" |
| व | va | "v/w" |
| स | sa | "s" |
| ह | ha | "h" |

## Example Sentences

- **कमल** (kamal) — lotus
- **राम** (rām) — Ram (a common name)
- **नाम** (nām) — name
- **पानी** (pānī) — water
- **घर** (ghar) — house
- **माँ** (mā̃) — mother

## Grammar / Script Notes

The vowels above are "independent" forms used at the start of a word; inside words, vowels other than inherent अ attach to consonants as matras (covered in the next lesson). Consonants are organized into five varga (groups) by point of articulation: kavarga (क ख ग घ ङ — velar), cavarga (च छ ज झ ञ — palatal), ṭavarga (ट ठ ड ढ ण — retroflex), tavarga (त थ द ध न — dental), and pavarga (प फ ब भ म — labial).

Each varga has an unaspirated voiceless, aspirated voiceless, unaspirated voiced, aspirated voiced, and a nasal — a four-way contrast missing from English (compare क ka / ख kha / ग ga / घ gha). Retroflex (ट ठ ड ढ) versus dental (त थ द ध) is also phonemic: कान (kān, ear) versus काँ (kā̃, crow-sound) differ; गुड़ (guṛ, jaggery) versus गुड (guḍ) sound distinct to Hindi ears.

## Common Mistakes

- Pronouncing त like English "t" — it is dental (tongue touches the teeth), not alveolar.
- Confusing aspirated and unaspirated pairs (क vs ख); in Hindi this changes the word.
- Forgetting that every consonant carries an implicit "a" — क alone reads "ka", not "k".

## Try It Yourself

1. Write your name in Devanagari using the consonants and matras you know.
2. Read aloud: कमल, पानी, राम, घर, माँ.
3. Find five Hindi shop signs (or images online) and identify the consonant varga of each first letter.
4. Compare the sounds of क/ख and ट/त by recording yourself.

## Next Steps

The next lesson covers matras (vowel signs) and conjunct consonants — the tools that turn isolated letters into actual Hindi words.

# Matras, Conjuncts & Numbers

Once you know the base consonants, matras (vowel signs) attach to them so consonants can carry vowels other than the default "a". Conjuncts join two consonants when no vowel sits between them. Hindi also has its own digits.

## Core Vocabulary

| Devanagari | Romanization | English |
|------------|--------------|---------|
| का | kā | "kaa" (क + ा) |
| कि | ki | "ki" (क + ि) |
| की | kī | "kii" (क + ी) |
| कु | ku | "ku" (क + ु) |
| कू | kū | "kuu" (क + ू) |
| के | ke | "ke" (क + े) |
| कै | kai | "kai" (क + ै) |
| को | ko | "ko" (क + ो) |
| कौ | kau | "kau" (क + ौ) |
| क् | k | bare consonant (halant ्) |
| क्ष | kṣa | conjunct क + ष |
| त्र | tra | conjunct त + र |
| ज्ञ | jña | conjunct ज + ञ |
| श्र | śra | conjunct श + र |
| ० | 0 | śūnya |
| १ | 1 | ek |
| २ | 2 | do |
| ३ | 3 | tīn |
| ४ | 4 | cār |
| ५ | 5 | pā̃c |
| ६ | 6 | chaḥ |
| ७ | 7 | sāt |
| ८ | 8 | āṭh |
| ९ | 9 | nau |
| १० | 10 | das |

## Example Sentences

- **किताब** (kitāb) — book (notice ि before क even though "ki" is read after)
- **दिल्ली** (dillī) — Delhi (दिल्ली uses the conjunct ल्ल)
- **विद्यालय** (vidyālay) — school (द्य = द + य conjunct)
- **मेरा नाम राम है** (merā nām rām hai) — My name is Ram.
- **यह २०२६ है** (yah 2026 hai) — This is 2026.

## Grammar / Script Notes

Matras attach in fixed positions: ा, ो, ौ, े, ै go to the right; ु, ू, ृ go below; ि goes to the left of its consonant even though it is pronounced after; ी goes to the right. The halant (्) under a consonant cancels its inherent "a" — used in dictionaries and to form conjuncts when a typesetter cannot stack glyphs.

Conjuncts represent consonant clusters with no vowel between them. Some are vertical stacks (द्ध = द + ध), some are horizontal (स्त = स + त), and a few have unique shapes — most importantly क्ष (kṣa), त्र (tra), ज्ञ (jña), and श्र (śra). You will see these constantly in everyday words: छात्र (chātra, student), विज्ञान (vijñān, science), क्षमा (kṣamā, forgiveness).

Hindi numerals (०१२३४५६७८९) are the ancestors of the Arabic-Indic and Western digits. Modern Hindi text mixes them freely with Western numerals; both forms are taught in Indian schools.

## Common Mistakes

- Writing ि after the consonant in romanization order — in Devanagari it sits to the *left* of its consonant.
- Treating हिन्दी and हिंदी as different words — anusvara ं is a common alternative to a nasal + halant cluster.
- Forgetting to drop the inherent "a" at word ends in modern Hindi: राम is read "Rām" not "Rāma".

## Try It Yourself

1. Write your phone number using Hindi digits.
2. Decompose: क्षत्रिय → क् + ष + त् + र + ि + य. Identify each conjunct.
3. Write पानी, घर, किताब without looking, then check matra positions.
4. Find any Hindi book cover and circle every conjunct you can identify.

## Next Steps

Next we work on pronunciation distinctions Hindi makes that English does not — aspiration and retroflexion.

# Pronunciation & Transliteration

Hindi has phonemic distinctions English speakers usually miss: aspirated vs unaspirated stops (क vs ख), retroflex vs dental (ट vs त), and nasalized vowels (हाँ vs हान). Getting these wrong changes meanings.

## Core Vocabulary

| Devanagari | Romanization | English |
|------------|--------------|---------|
| कान | kān | ear |
| खान | khān | mine (noun) / Khan |
| गाना | gānā | song / to sing |
| घर | ghar | house |
| चाय | cāy | tea |
| छह | chaḥ | six |
| जल | jal | water |
| झूठ | jhūṭh | lie (untruth) |
| टमाटर | ṭamāṭar | tomato |
| ठीक | ṭhīk | OK / fine |
| डर | ḍar | fear |
| ढक्कन | ḍhakkan | lid |
| तीन | tīn | three |
| थाली | thālī | plate |
| दिन | din | day |
| धन्यवाद | dhanyavād | thank you |
| पानी | pānī | water |
| फल | phal | fruit |
| बाल | bāl | hair |
| भाई | bhāī | brother |
| हाँ | hā̃ | yes (nasalized) |
| हान | hān | (rare; non-nasal) |
| ज़रा | zarā | a little (nuqta) |
| फ़ोन | phon/fon | phone (nuqta) |

## Example Sentences

- **मैं ठीक हूँ।** (mai ṭhīk hū̃) — I am fine.
- **यह पानी है।** (yah pānī hai) — This is water.
- **धन्यवाद!** (dhanyavād) — Thank you!
- **फल खाओ।** (phal khāo) — Eat fruit.
- **मेरा भाई गाना गाता है।** (merā bhāī gānā gātā hai) — My brother sings.

## Grammar / Script Notes

Aspirated consonants (ख, घ, छ, झ, ठ, ढ, थ, ध, फ, भ) carry an audible puff of air — hold a hand in front of your mouth and you should feel a burst on ख that you do not feel on क. Most aspirated/unaspirated pairs are minimal pairs in Hindi.

Retroflex consonants (ट, ठ, ड, ढ, ण) are made with the tongue tip curled back to touch the roof of the mouth; dentals (त, थ, द, ध, न) are made with the tongue tip on the back of the upper teeth. English "t" and "d" sound somewhere between the two — choose the wrong one in Hindi and you'll be misunderstood.

Nasalization is marked by candrabindu (ँ) over the vowel, e.g. हाँ (hā̃, yes) versus हान. The anusvara (ं) is used before stops (हिंदी = hindī) and is realized as the matching nasal of the following consonant. The dot under a letter (nuqta) — क़, ख़, ग़, ज़, फ़, ड़, ढ़ — marks Persian/Arabic loan sounds (q, x, ɣ, z, f) and tap-flap retroflexes; in casual writing the dot is often dropped.

Standard romanization schemes include IAST (used here, with macrons and dots) and ITRANS (capital letters for retroflex/aspirate). Hindi-English transliteration in WhatsApp messages is informal — "kya kar rahe ho" for क्या कर रहे हो — and conventions vary.

## Common Mistakes

- Pronouncing थ like English "th" in "thanks" — it is aspirated dental "t", not a fricative.
- Using English "t/d" for Hindi त/द — they sound dental-Spanish, not alveolar-English.
- Dropping nasalization: कहाँ (kahā̃, where) vs कहा (kahā, said) are different verbs/words.

## Try It Yourself

1. Record yourself saying कान / खान / गान / घान — listen for the aspiration.
2. Practice ट / त minimal pairs: टीन (tin can) vs तीन (three).
3. Find five English loanwords in Hindi and note whether they use the nuqta (फ़ोन, ज़ोन).
4. Read aloud: मेरा भाई फल खाता है।

## Next Steps

With sounds and script in place, the next unit moves to grammar — starting with Hindi's two-gender system and its postpositions.

# Gender, Number & Postpositions

Every Hindi noun is masculine or feminine, and adjectives, verbs, and postpositions agree with the noun. Hindi has no prepositions; it has postpositions (words that come *after* the noun) like का, को, में, से, पर.

## Core Vocabulary

| Devanagari | Romanization | English |
|------------|--------------|---------|
| लड़का | laṛkā | boy (m) |
| लड़की | laṛkī | girl (f) |
| किताब | kitāb | book (f) |
| मेज़ | mez | table (f) |
| कुर्सी | kursī | chair (f) |
| कमरा | kamrā | room (m) |
| घर | ghar | house (m) |
| पानी | pānī | water (m) |
| दूध | dūdh | milk (m) |
| रोटी | roṭī | bread/roti (f) |
| का / की / के | kā / kī / ke | of (possessive postposition) |
| को | ko | to / direct object marker |
| में | me͂ | in |
| पर | par | on |
| से | se | from / by / with |
| तक | tak | up to / until |
| के लिए | ke lie | for |
| के पास | ke pās | near / with (in possession) |

## Example Sentences

- **लड़का घर में है।** (laṛkā ghar me͂ hai) — The boy is in the house.
- **लड़की किताब पढ़ती है।** (laṛkī kitāb paṛhtī hai) — The girl reads a book.
- **यह राम का घर है।** (yah rām kā ghar hai) — This is Ram's house.
- **मेज़ पर पानी है।** (mez par pānī hai) — There is water on the table.
- **मैं स्कूल से आ रहा हूँ।** (mai͂ skūl se ā rahā hū̃) — I am coming from school.
- **मेरे पास एक कुत्ता है।** (mere pās ek kuttā hai) — I have a dog. (literally: "near me there is a dog")

## Grammar / Script Notes

Most masculine nouns end in -ā (लड़का, कमरा, कुत्ता) and pluralize to -e (लड़के, कमरे). Most feminine nouns end in -ī (लड़की, रोटी) and pluralize to -iyā̃ (लड़कियाँ, रोटियाँ). Many nouns do not follow this pattern — किताब (book) is feminine despite ending in a consonant, मकान (house) is masculine. Gender must be memorized with the noun.

Postpositions trigger the **oblique case** on the preceding noun: लड़का (direct, "boy") becomes लड़के in लड़के को (to the boy), लड़के से (from the boy). Plural masculines end in -ओं in oblique (लड़कों को). Feminines ending in -ī take -iyo͂ in oblique plural (लड़कियों को). The oblique form is invisible on most "irregular" nouns but is real grammatically.

का / की / के agrees with the *possessed* item, not the possessor: राम का घर (Ram's house, m sg), राम की किताब (Ram's book, f sg), राम के घर (Ram's houses, m pl). Think of it as a special adjective.

Hindi has no verb "to have" — possession is expressed with के पास (near) for movable things, का (of) for relatives and body parts: मेरे दो भाई हैं (I have two brothers, lit. "of-mine two brothers are").

## Common Mistakes

- Saying *लड़का को* instead of लड़के को (forgetting the oblique).
- Using का with a feminine noun: *राम का किताब* — should be राम की किताब.
- Translating "I have a book" as *मैं एक किताब है* — use मेरे पास एक किताब है.

## Try It Yourself

1. Make three sentences using में, पर, and से with kitchen objects.
2. Convert to oblique: कमरा → ___ में; कुर्सी → ___ पर; लड़के → ___ को.
3. Translate: "The girl's book is on the table."
4. List five family members with their gender.

## Next Steps

Now that nouns and postpositions agree, the next lesson builds verbs that also agree — Hindi present tense.

# Present Tense & Verb Structure

Hindi verbs end in -ना in dictionary form (the infinitive). To conjugate, drop -ना to get the root, then add a participle ending agreeing with subject's gender and number, plus a form of होना (to be) for tense.

## Core Vocabulary

| Devanagari | Romanization | English |
|------------|--------------|---------|
| होना | honā | to be |
| करना | karnā | to do |
| जाना | jānā | to go |
| आना | ānā | to come |
| खाना | khānā | to eat |
| पीना | pīnā | to drink |
| पढ़ना | paṛhnā | to read / study |
| लिखना | likhnā | to write |
| बोलना | bolnā | to speak |
| देखना | dekhnā | to see / watch |
| सुनना | sunnā | to listen |
| सोना | sonā | to sleep |
| रहना | rahnā | to stay / live |
| हूँ | hū̃ | am |
| है | hai | is |
| हैं | hai͂ | are |
| हो | ho | are (familiar) |
| रहा / रही / रहे | rahā / rahī / rahe | -ing (continuous marker) |

## Example Sentences

- **मैं हिन्दी पढ़ता हूँ।** (mai͂ hindī paṛhtā hū̃) — I (m) study Hindi. (habitual)
- **मैं हिन्दी पढ़ती हूँ।** (mai͂ hindī paṛhtī hū̃) — I (f) study Hindi.
- **वह चाय पीता है।** (vah cāy pītā hai) — He drinks tea.
- **हम स्कूल जाते हैं।** (ham skūl jāte hai͂) — We go to school.
- **मैं अभी खाना खा रहा हूँ।** (mai͂ abhī khānā khā rahā hū̃) — I am eating right now.
- **तुम क्या कर रहे हो?** (tum kyā kar rahe ho?) — What are you doing?
- **वे यहाँ रहते हैं।** (ve yahā̃ rahte hai͂) — They live here.

## Grammar / Script Notes

**Present habitual**: drop -ना, add -ता (m sg) / -ती (f sg) / -ते (m pl, also formal) / -ती (f pl), then a present form of होना. So करना → करता हूँ / करती हूँ / करते हैं / करती हैं depending on the subject.

**Present continuous**: root + रहा/रही/रहे + है/हूँ/हैं. Use this for "right now" actions: मैं खा रहा हूँ (I am eating). Habitual उससे करना और continuous करते रहना are distinct in Hindi where English uses one tense.

The auxiliary होना is irregular: मैं हूँ, तू है, तुम हो, वह है, हम हैं, आप हैं, वे हैं. Note तुम hai different ending than वह; this is a politeness/level distinction (next lesson).

Word order is strictly **Subject – Object – Verb**, with the auxiliary at the very end: मैं [S] रोटी [O] खा [V root] रहा हूँ [aux]. Adverbs and time expressions slot before the verb.

## Common Mistakes

- Mixing male and female forms: a woman should say पढ़ती हूँ, not पढ़ता हूँ.
- Forgetting the auxiliary: *मैं पढ़ता* on its own is incomplete — needs हूँ.
- Putting the verb mid-sentence: English "I read books at home" → Hindi मैं घर पर किताबें पढ़ता हूँ (verb goes last).

## Try It Yourself

1. Conjugate बोलना in present habitual for मैं (m), मैं (f), हम, वह.
2. Convert to continuous: मैं चाय पीता हूँ → ?
3. Write three sentences about your morning routine.
4. Translate: "She is writing a letter."

## Next Steps

Verbs change with politeness level too. Next: pronouns, the three "you"s, and respect.

# Pronouns & Respect Levels

Hindi has three "you"s — तू (intimate), तुम (familiar), and आप (respectful) — and they trigger different verb endings. Pronouns also change form before postpositions (oblique case).

## Core Vocabulary

| Devanagari | Romanization | English |
|------------|--------------|---------|
| मैं | mai͂ | I |
| तू | tū | you (very intimate / to a child / to god) |
| तुम | tum | you (familiar, friends, juniors) |
| आप | āp | you (respectful, plural) |
| यह / ये | yah / ye | this / he-she-it (near) / they |
| वह / वे | vah / ve | that / he-she-it (far) / they |
| हम | ham | we |
| मेरा / मेरी / मेरे | merā/merī/mere | my |
| तुम्हारा | tumhārā | your (familiar) |
| आपका | āpkā | your (respectful) |
| उसका | uskā | his / her |
| उनका | unkā | their / his/her (respectful) |
| मुझे / मुझको | mujhe / mujhko | to me / me (object) |
| तुम्हें | tumhe͂ | to you (familiar) |
| आपको | āpko | to you (respectful) |
| उसे / उसको | use / usko | to him / her |

## Example Sentences

- **तू कहाँ है?** (tū kahā̃ hai?) — Where are you? (to a child)
- **तुम कैसे हो?** (tum kaise ho?) — How are you? (friend)
- **आप कैसे हैं?** (āp kaise hai͂?) — How are you? (respectful)
- **यह मेरी बहन है।** (yah merī bahan hai) — This is my sister.
- **उसका नाम क्या है?** (uskā nām kyā hai?) — What is his/her name?
- **मुझे चाय पसंद है।** (mujhe cāy pasand hai) — I like tea. (lit. "to me, tea is pleasing")
- **आपको क्या चाहिए?** (āpko kyā cāhie?) — What do you need?

## Grammar / Script Notes

Each "you" takes a distinct verb conjugation in present tense: तू है / तू करता है, तुम हो / तुम करते हो (always plural-marked verb!), आप हैं / आप करते हैं. Even when speaking to one person, तुम and आप use plural verb forms; this is grammaticalized respect, not number.

When a pronoun is followed by a postposition, it shifts to its **oblique** form: मैं → मुझ (मुझ + को = मुझे/मुझको), तू → तुझ, यह → इस, वह → उस, हम → हम, तुम → तुम, आप → आप, ये → इन, वे → उन. So "from him" is उससे (उस + से), "in this" is इसमें.

Possessive adjectives (मेरा, तुम्हारा, आपका, उसका, हमारा, उनका) agree like adjectives ending in -ā: merā ghar (m sg), merī kitāb (f sg), mere bhāī (m pl), merī kitābe͂ (f pl). उसका can mean "his" or "her" — Hindi does not mark gender on third-person pronouns, only on the verb agreement with the subject.

For respectful third-person reference, use वे/उन: मेरे पिताजी हिन्दी पढ़ाते हैं — "My father teaches Hindi" (using plural ending पढ़ाते हैं as a sign of respect for one parent).

## Common Mistakes

- Using तू with a stranger or boss — it is rude in most contexts.
- Saying *तुम है* — तुम always takes plural-style verbs (तुम हो, तुम करते हो).
- Forgetting that "to like" is मुझे ... पसंद है, not *मैं ... पसंद करता हूँ* (which means "I prefer/choose").

## Try It Yourself

1. Address your best friend, your grandmother, and your boss with the right pronoun + verb form for "How are you?".
2. Replace nouns with pronouns: राम का भाई → ___ का भाई.
3. Translate: "I like Hindi food." (use मुझे)
4. Make three सेंटेंस using oblique pronouns + postpositions.

## Next Steps

With pronouns set, we shift to vocabulary — starting with family, food, and home.

# Family, Food & Home

Family terms in Hindi distinguish maternal vs paternal sides and elder vs younger siblings — relationships that English collapses. Indian food vocabulary is rich and very useful even in English-speaking contexts.

## Core Vocabulary

| Devanagari | Romanization | English |
|------------|--------------|---------|
| पिता / पिताजी | pitā / pitājī | father |

| दादा / दादी | dādā / dādī | paternal grandfather/mother |
| नाना / नानी | nānā / nānī | maternal grandfather/mother |
| चाचा / चाची | cācā / cācī | paternal uncle/aunt |
| मामा / मामी | māmā / māmī | maternal uncle/aunt |
| बेटा / बेटी | beṭā / beṭī | son / daughter |
| पति / पत्नी | pati / patnī | husband / wife |

| रसोई | rasoī | kitchen |

| दरवाज़ा | darvāzā | door |

## Example Sentences

- **मेरे पिताजी डॉक्टर हैं।** (mere pitājī ḍākṭar hai͂) — My father is a doctor.
- **उसकी माँ खाना बना रही हैं।** (uskī mā̃ khānā banā rahī hai͂) — His mother is cooking.
- **मेरे दो बड़े भाई हैं।** (mere do baṛe bhāī hai͂) — I have two elder brothers.
- **मुझे दाल-चावल पसंद है।** (mujhe dāl-cāval pasand hai) — I like dal and rice.
- **रसोई में दूध है।** (rasoī me͂ dūdh hai) — There is milk in the kitchen.
- **दादी कहानी सुनाती हैं।** (dādī kahānī sunātī hai͂) — Grandmother tells a story.

## Grammar / Script Notes

Indian kinship makes a sharp paternal-vs-maternal distinction: दादा-दादी (father's parents) vs नाना-नानी (mother's parents); चाचा (father's younger brother) vs मामा (mother's brother) vs ताऊ (father's elder brother) vs फूफा (father's sister's husband). When learning, always pair the term with which side it refers to — confusion is a real social misstep at family gatherings.

Adding -जी to a kin term or name signals respect: पिताजी, माताजी, भैयाजी, रामजी. Many speakers also use the plural verb with one parent as honorific (मेरी माँ कहती हैं, "my mother says"). Both devices are common, especially in writing and in conservative households.

Food terms are mostly feminine (दाल, सब्ज़ी, रोटी, चाय) but दूध (milk) and चावल (rice) are masculine. Compounds are common: दाल-चावल (dal and rice), चाय-नाश्ता (tea and snack).

## Common Mistakes

- Calling your mother's brother *चाचा* — use मामा.
- Treating दूध as feminine — it is masculine: ठंडा दूध, not *ठंडी दूध*.
- Asking "are you married?" with तू — use आप शादीशुदा हैं? unless very close.

## Try It Yourself

1. Draw your family tree and label every person in Hindi.
2. List five Hindi food words you already use in English (chai, roti, dal, ...).
3. Describe your room: मेरे कमरे में ... है।
4. Make a sentence with three kin terms.

## Next Steps

Next we cover vocabulary for the body, health, and emotions — useful for doctor visits and everyday conversation.

# Body, Health & Emotions

Body-part and emotion vocabulary lets you describe how you feel and what hurts — both essential for doctor visits and everyday conversation. Hindi often uses "X is on/in me" structures rather than "I have X".

## Core Vocabulary

| Devanagari | Romanization | English |
|------------|--------------|---------|
| सिर | sir | head |
| बाल | bāl | hair |
| आँख | ā̃kh | eye |
| नाक | nāk | nose |
| कान | kān | ear |
| मुँह | mu̇̃h | mouth |
| दाँत | dā̃t | tooth |
| गला | galā | throat |
| हाथ | hāth | hand / arm |
| पैर | pair | foot / leg |
| पेट | peṭ | stomach |
| दिल | dil | heart |
| बीमार | bīmār | sick |
| बुख़ार | bukhār | fever |
| दर्द | dard | pain |
| सर्दी | sardī | cold (illness) / winter |
| दवा | davā | medicine |
| डॉक्टर | ḍākṭar | doctor |
| ख़ुश | khuś | happy |
| उदास | udās | sad |
| ग़ुस्सा | gussā | anger |
| डर | ḍar | fear |
| थका हुआ | thakā huā | tired (m) |
| भूखा / भूखी | bhūkhā / bhūkhī | hungry (m/f) |
| प्यासा / प्यासी | pyāsā / pyāsī | thirsty (m/f) |

## Example Sentences

- **मेरे सिर में दर्द है।** (mere sir me͂ dard hai) — I have a headache. (lit. "in my head pain is")
- **मुझे बुख़ार है।** (mujhe bukhār hai) — I have a fever.
- **उसे सर्दी हो गई है।** (use sardī ho gaī hai) — She has caught a cold.
- **मैं बहुत ख़ुश हूँ।** (mai͂ bahut khuś hū̃) — I am very happy.
- **वह उदास क्यों है?** (vah udās kyo͂ hai?) — Why is he sad?
- **मुझे भूख लगी है।** (mujhe bhūkh lagī hai) — I am hungry. (lit. "to me hunger has struck")
- **डॉक्टर से मिलो।** (ḍākṭar se milo) — Go meet a doctor.

## Grammar / Script Notes

Many physical sensations and emotions in Hindi use the "**X-ko Y है / लगता है**" pattern, where the experiencer is in the dative (-को): मुझे ठंड लग रही है (I am feeling cold), उसे डर लगता है (he feels scared). The subject grammatically is the sensation, not the person.

Pain is expressed with में: मेरे पेट में दर्द है (I have a stomachache, "in my stomach pain is"). Adding होना forms perfective: सिर में दर्द हो गया (a headache started/has come on).

Adjectives like भूखा, प्यासा, थका हुआ agree in gender and number with the noun they describe: एक भूखा लड़का, एक भूखी लड़की. The phrase थका हुआ literally is a participle "having become tired" — हुआ also agrees.

## Common Mistakes

- Saying *मैं भूखा हूँ* is grammatical but the more idiomatic phrase is मुझे भूख लगी है.
- Treating दर्द as a verb — it is a noun. Use ... में दर्द है.
- Mixing pair (foot) with another word — पैर covers leg + foot together.

## Try It Yourself

1. Tell your doctor: "I have a sore throat and a fever."
2. Express with -को: hungry, thirsty, cold, scared (use लग- verb).
3. Make a sentence with three body parts.
4. Translate: "Why is he angry?"

## Next Steps

Next we expand into school, work, and city vocabulary — the language of public life.

# School, Work & City

Vocabulary for education, jobs, transport, and getting around the city. These are the words that fill conversations at the office, in classrooms, on the metro, and at intersections.

## Core Vocabulary

| Devanagari | Romanization | English |
|------------|--------------|---------|
| स्कूल / विद्यालय | skūl / vidyālay | school |

| परीक्षा | parīkṣā | exam |
| दफ़्तर | daftar | office |
| काम | kām | work |
| नौकरी | naukrī | job |
| डॉक्टर | ḍākṭar | doctor |
| इंजीनियर | i͂jīniyar | engineer |
| दुकान | dukān | shop |
| बाज़ार | bāzār | market |
| सड़क | saṛak | road |
| गली | galī | lane / alley |
| रेल / ट्रेन | rel / ṭren | train |
| बस | bas | bus |

| रिक्शा | rikśā | rickshaw |

| अस्पताल | aspatāl | hospital |
| बैंक | bai͂k | bank |

## Example Sentences

- **मैं विद्यार्थी हूँ।** (mai͂ vidyārthī hū̃) — I am a student.
- **वह दिल्ली विश्वविद्यालय में पढ़ती है।** (vah dillī viśvavidyālay me͂ paṛhtī hai) — She studies at Delhi University.
- **मेरी नौकरी एक बैंक में है।** (merī naukrī ek bai͂k me͂ hai) — My job is at a bank.
- **बाज़ार जाने के लिए मेट्रो लो।** (bāzār jāne ke lie meṭro lo) — Take the metro to go to the market.
- **अस्पताल यहाँ से कितनी दूर है?** (aspatāl yahā̃ se kitnī dūr hai?) — How far is the hospital from here?
- **रिक्शा वाले से बात करो।** (rikśā vāle se bāt karo) — Talk to the rickshaw driver.

## Grammar / Script Notes

The suffix **-वाला / -वाली** turns a noun into "the X person" or "the X one": रिक्शावाला (rickshaw guy), दूधवाला (milkman), चायवाली (tea-seller, f). It is one of Hindi's most productive suffixes: हिन्दी बोलनेवाला (a Hindi-speaking person), लाल कमीज़वाला (the guy in the red shirt).

Many modern domain words are direct English borrowings written in Devanagari: स्कूल, कॉलेज, ऑफ़िस, ट्रेन, मेट्रो, बस. They keep English-style invariant plurals in casual speech (ट्रेनें in formal Hindi, just ट्रेन in colloquial). Sanskrit-origin equivalents (विद्यालय, महाविद्यालय, कार्यालय) are common in formal writing and signage.

To say "going to / coming from" a place, use जाना/आना with में or को: मैं स्कूल जा रहा हूँ (I am going to school — को is often dropped before institutions). से = "from": मैं काम से आ रहा हूँ (I am coming from work).

## Common Mistakes

- Forgetting that काम = work in general; नौकरी = a salaried job.
- Using *पढ़ाई* (studies) and *पढ़ना* (to read/study) interchangeably — पढ़ाई is the noun.
- Writing English loanwords as if they were native Hindi — ऑफिस and दफ़्तर coexist; choose register accordingly.

## Try It Yourself

1. Describe what you do for work in two sentences.
2. Form three -वाला words for people in your neighborhood.
3. Ask: "Where is the nearest metro station?" (मेट्रो स्टेशन)
4. Translate: "Students take the bus to college."

## Next Steps

We've covered key noun fields. Time to put them to use in conversation — starting with greetings.

# Greetings & Self-Introduction

Hindi greetings carry religious and cultural connotations. नमस्ते is the universal default, but you'll also hear सलाम / आदाब (Muslim greeting), सत श्री अकाल (Sikh greeting), and English-style hello in cities.

## Core Vocabulary

| Devanagari | Romanization | English |
|------------|--------------|---------|
| नमस्ते | namaste | hello (universal) |
| नमस्कार | namaskār | hello (formal) |
| सलाम / आदाब | salām / ādāb | peace (Muslim greeting) |
| सत श्री अकाल | sat śrī akāl | Sikh greeting |
| शुभ प्रभात | śubh prabhāt | good morning (formal) |
| शुभ रात्रि | śubh rātri | good night |
| धन्यवाद | dhanyavād | thank you |
| शुक्रिया | śukriyā | thank you (Urdu-influenced) |
| माफ़ कीजिए | māf kījie | excuse me / sorry |
| जी हाँ / जी नहीं | jī hā̃ / jī nahī͂ | yes / no (polite) |
| मेरा नाम ... है | merā nām ... hai | my name is ... |
| आपका नाम क्या है? | āpkā nām kyā hai? | what is your name? |
| मैं ... से हूँ | mai͂ ... se hū̃ | I am from ... |
| आप कैसे हैं? | āp kaise hai͂? | how are you? (m) |
| आप कैसी हैं? | āp kaisī hai͂? | how are you? (f) |
| मैं ठीक हूँ | mai͂ ṭhīk hū̃ | I'm fine |
| मिलकर ख़ुशी हुई | milkar khuśī huī | nice to meet you |
| फिर मिलेंगे | phir mile͂ge | see you again |
| अलविदा | alvidā | goodbye |

## Example Sentences

- **नमस्ते! मेरा नाम प्रिया है।** (namaste! merā nām priyā hai) — Hello! My name is Priya.
- **आपका शुभ नाम क्या है?** (āpkā śubh nām kyā hai?) — What is your good name? (very polite)
- **मैं अमेरिका से हूँ।** (mai͂ amerikā se hū̃) — I am from America.
- **मैं छात्र हूँ।** (mai͂ chātra hū̃) — I am a student.
- **आप कहाँ रहते हैं?** (āp kahā̃ rahte hai͂?) — Where do you live? (to a man)
- **मिलकर बहुत ख़ुशी हुई।** (milkar bahut khuśī huī) — Very nice to meet you.

## Grammar / Script Notes

नमस्ते is from Sanskrit नमः (bow) + ते (to you). The same word covers hello and goodbye, like Italian ciao. नमस्कार is its more formal sibling, common in offices and TV news. Add -जी after a name for respect: रामजी, प्रियाजी.

When introducing yourself, women say मैं ... हूँ with feminine-agreeing nouns/adjectives: मैं भारतीय हूँ works for both, but मैं बीमार हूँ (m) vs मैं बीमार हूँ also works because बीमार is invariant; मैं थका हूँ (m) vs मैं थकी हूँ (f) is variable. Watch your -आ / -ई endings.

The polite phrase आपका शुभ नाम (literally "your auspicious name") is a North Indian convention; in Hindi-Urdu Lucknowi style it is the default at first meeting. आदाब + a hand gesture is a respectful salaam used in Muslim and Hyderabadi contexts.

## Common Mistakes

- Saying नमस्ते जी — it's already polite; जी is redundant after greeting words.
- Replying *मैं अच्छा हूँ* literally for "I am good" — say मैं ठीक हूँ instead.
- Using तू with someone you just met — even अंकल/आंटी on the street get आप.

## Try It Yourself

1. Introduce yourself in 4 sentences: name, where you're from, what you do, why you're learning Hindi.
2. Ask three questions you would ask a new acquaintance.
3. Practice with a partner: greet, exchange names, say goodbye.
4. Try नमस्कार in a more formal setting — does it feel different?

## Next Steps

Next: shopping and bargaining, where Hindi gets practical and number-heavy.

# Shopping & Bargaining

Indian markets reward bargaining (मोल भाव). Knowing prices, polite refusals, and quantity words turns a stressful exchange into a friendly one.

## Core Vocabulary

| दुकान | dukān | shop |
| दुकानदार | dukāndār | shopkeeper |
| ग्राहक | grāhak | customer |
| क़ीमत / दाम | qīmat / dām | price |
| रुपया / रुपये | rupayā / rupaye | rupee / rupees |
| पैसा | paisā | money / paisa (1/100 rupee) |
| सस्ता / सस्ती | sastā / sastī | cheap (m/f) |
| महँगा / महँगी | mahã̄gā / mahã̄gī | expensive (m/f) |
| थोड़ा कम | thoṛā kam | a little less |
| ज़्यादा | zyādā | more / too much |
| कितना? / कितनी? | kitnā / kitnī | how much? (m/f) |
| एक किलो | ek kilo | one kilo |
| आधा किलो | ādhā kilo | half a kilo |
| दो सौ | do sau | two hundred |
| एक हज़ार | ek hazār | one thousand |
| दिखाइए | dikhāie | please show |
| दीजिए | dījie | please give |
| ले लूँगा / ले लूँगी | le lū̃gā / le lū̃gī | I'll take it (m/f) |
| रहने दीजिए | rahne dījie | leave it / never mind |
| बिल | bil | bill |
| रसीद | rasīd | receipt |

## Example Sentences

- **यह कितने का है?** (yah kitne kā hai?) — How much is this?
- **यह बहुत महँगा है।** (yah bahut mahã̄gā hai) — This is very expensive.
- **थोड़ा कम कीजिए।** (thoṛā kam kījie) — Please reduce a little.
- **दो सौ रुपये में दे दीजिए।** (do sau rupaye me͂ de dījie) — Give it for two hundred rupees.
- **ठीक है, मैं ले लूँगी।** (ṭhīk hai, mai͂ le lū̃gī) — OK, I'll take it. (f speaker)
- **रसीद दे दीजिए।** (rasīd de dījie) — Please give the receipt.

## Grammar / Script Notes

Prices use **का/की/के + value**: यह सौ रुपये का है (this is of one hundred rupees). For "for X rupees" use में: सौ रुपये में दे दो (give it for 100 rupees). The construction X रुपये का / की / के agrees with the gendered item being priced.

Polite imperatives end in **-इए**: दीजिए (give), लीजिए (take), बताइए (tell), आइए (come). The -इए form is used with आप; -ओ is the तुम familiar form (दो, बताओ); the bare root is the तू form (दे, बता). Match your imperative to the level of address you've already established.

Hindi numbers above 100 are unpredictable — 21 इक्कीस, 33 तैंतीस, 47 सैंतालीस — and have no obvious pattern in tens-units. Memorize the round numbers first (दस, बीस, तीस, चालीस, पचास, साठ, सत्तर, अस्सी, नब्बे, सौ).

## Common Mistakes

- Asking *कितना है?* for a feminine item — use कितनी है? (e.g. साड़ी for sari).
- Saying *रुपया* for plural — it's रुपये (oblique form) in रुपये में.
- Refusing too softly — Indian shopkeepers expect a firm रहने दीजिए if you don't want it.

## Try It Yourself

1. Bargain a price down from ५०० to ३०० in three exchanges.
2. Ask the price of: a kilo of mangoes, a saree, a notebook.
3. Refuse politely twice without buying.
4. Translate: "How much is half a kilo of tomatoes?"

## Next Steps

Next we move from transactional to expressive language — opinions, agreement, and requests.

# Expressing Opinions & Requests

To make polite requests, agree, disagree, or share an opinion in Hindi, you'll combine modal-like verbs (सकना, चाहिए, चाहना) with idiomatic phrases.

| बिल्कुल | bilkul | absolutely |
| सही | sahī | correct / right |
| ग़लत | galat | wrong |
| हाँ, सच है | hā̃, sac hai | yes, it's true |
| मैं सहमत हूँ | mai͂ sahmat hū̃ | I agree |
| मैं असहमत हूँ | mai͂ asahmat hū̃ | I disagree |
| क्या आप ... सकते हैं? | kyā āp ... sakte hai͂? | could you ...? |
| ... चाहिए | ... cāhie | (something) is needed / wanted |
| कृपया | kṛpayā | please |
| ज़रा | zarā | just / a little (softener) |
| बताइए | batāie | please tell |
| माफ़ कीजिए | māf kījie | excuse me / sorry |
| मुझे ... पसंद है | mujhe ... pasand hai | I like ... |
| मुझे ... पसंद नहीं है | mujhe ... pasand nahī͂ hai | I don't like ... |
| अच्छा / बुरा | acchā / burā | good / bad |

## Example Sentences

- **मुझे लगता है कि यह सही है।** (mujhe lagtā hai ki yah sahī hai) — I think this is correct.
- **मेरे ख़याल से दिल्ली बेहतर है।** (mere khayāl se dillī behtar hai) — In my opinion, Delhi is better.
- **क्या आप मेरी मदद कर सकते हैं?** (kyā āp merī madad kar sakte hai͂?) — Could you help me?
- **मुझे एक गिलास पानी चाहिए।** (mujhe ek gilās pānī cāhie) — I need a glass of water.
- **कृपया दरवाज़ा बंद कीजिए।** (kṛpayā darvāzā band kījie) — Please close the door.
- **ज़रा यह देखिए।** (zarā yah dekhie) — Just look at this.
- **मुझे यह फ़िल्म पसंद नहीं है।** (mujhe yah film pasand nahī͂ hai) — I don't like this film.

## Grammar / Script Notes

**सकना** ("to be able") attaches to a verb stem and conjugates: मैं कर सकता हूँ (I can do), क्या आप बोल सकते हैं? (can you speak?). It is the standard Hindi modal for ability and permission requests.

**चाहिए** is invariant — "is needed" — and the wanter is in the dative: मुझे एक किताब चाहिए (I need a book). For "want to do" use the infinitive + चाहिए: मुझे जाना चाहिए (I should/need to go), or चाहना as a regular verb: मैं जाना चाहता हूँ (I want to go).

**मुझे ... पसंद है** — literally "to me, X is pleasing" — is the standard "I like" in Hindi. The disliked thing is grammatically the subject (so the verb agrees with it): मुझे ये किताबें पसंद हैं (I like these books, plural verb).

To soften any request, sprinkle in ज़रा (just), कृपया (please, formal), and the polite imperative -इए form. कृपया is mostly written; in speech most people just use the -इए ending and tone.

- *मैं पसंद करता हूँ* means "I prefer/choose", not "I like". Use मुझे पसंद है for "I like".
- Forgetting the verb agrees with the *thing* in liking constructions: मुझे चाय पसंद है (sg) vs मुझे चाय और कॉफ़ी पसंद हैं (pl).
- Using *कर* instead of conjugated कर सकता हूँ — सकना must be conjugated.

1. Express an opinion about your city using मेरे ख़याल से.
2. Make three polite requests using क्या आप ... सकते हैं?
3. Say what you want and don't want at a restaurant (चाहिए / पसंद).
4. Translate: "I think Hindi grammar is interesting."

| समाचार | samācār | news |

| लेख | lekh | article |

| विज्ञापन | vijñāpan | advertisement |
| पुस्तक | pustak | book (Sanskrit-origin) |
| मेनू | menu | menu |
| शाकाहारी | śākāhārī | vegetarian |
| मांसाहारी | mā̃sāhārī | non-vegetarian |
| गली | galī | lane |
| सड़क | saṛak | road |
| प्रवेश | praveś | entry |
| निकास | nikās | exit |
| बंद / खुला | band / khulā | closed / open |
| सावधान | sāvdhān | caution |
| धीरे | dhīre | slow / gently |
| प्रयोग | prayog | use |
| संख्या | saṅkhyā | number |

## Example Sentences

- **आज का मुख्य समाचार क्या है?** (āj kā mukhya samācār kyā hai?) — What's today's main news?
- **यह दुकान बंद है।** (yah dukān band hai) — This shop is closed.
- **मेनू में सब शाकाहारी है।** (menu me͂ sab śākāhārī hai) — Everything on the menu is vegetarian.
- **धीरे चलिए, स्कूल है।** (dhīre calie, skūl hai) — Drive slowly, there's a school.
- **प्रवेश इस ओर से।** (praveś is or se) — Entry from this side.

## Grammar / Script Notes

Hindi headlines compress aggressively. Verbs are often dropped entirely: "दिल्ली में बारिश" (Delhi me͂ bāriś — "Rain in Delhi") instead of दिल्ली में बारिश हुई. Date and place are dropped to the byline. To read fast, identify the noun chain first, then guess the implied verb.

Common Hindi-Urdu doublets you'll see in the wild: समाचार/अख़बार (news), पुस्तक/किताब (book), विद्यालय/स्कूल (school), जल/पानी (water), मार्ग/रास्ता/सड़क (road). Sanskrit-leaning text (government, academia) tends toward the first; spoken/colloquial uses the second; English loans like ऑफ़िस, मेट्रो, ब्लॉग fill in modern domains.

Devanagari has no capitals, so proper nouns require context: नरेन्द्र मोदी, गांधी, अमेज़ॉन look the same as common nouns. Quotation marks ( "..." or « ... ») bracket dialogue. Sentences end with the danda। (the vertical bar). Modern punctuation also uses commas, question marks, and periods.

## Common Mistakes

- Reading every consonant with its inherent "a" — modern Hindi drops most word-final and many internal अ. कमरा is "kamrā" not "kamarā".
- Skipping the danda — it is the full stop in Hindi, equivalent to "."
- Assuming पुस्तक and किताब are different things — they're synonyms, register-tagged.

# Writing Practice

Devanagari handwriting follows a top-bar (शिरोरेखा) tradition: write the body of the letter first, then add the horizontal bar last to connect a word's letters. Stroke order is mostly top-to-bottom, left-to-right.

| उत्तर | uttar | answer |
| प्रश्न | praśn | question |
| पैराग्राफ़ | pairāgrāph | paragraph (loanword) |

## Example Sentences

- **मेरे पास एक नई किताब है।** (mere pās ek naī kitāb hai) — I have a new book.
- **प्रिय पिताजी, मैं अच्छा हूँ।** (priya pitājī, mai͂ acchā hū̃) — Dear father, I am well.
- **विद्यालय में आज छुट्टी है।** (vidyālay me͂ āj chuṭṭī hai) — There is a holiday at school today.
- **यह मेरा पहला अनुच्छेद है।** (yah merā pahlā anucched hai) — This is my first paragraph.
- **कृपया अपना नाम लिखें।** (kṛpayā apnā nām likhe͂) — Please write your name.

## Grammar / Script Notes

In handwriting, write each letter's body first (vertical stem, curves, descenders), then connect them with one continuous शिरोरेखा. Conjuncts often skip the shirorekha bridge — क्ष and त्र, for example, are written as a single ligature. Matras attach in their fixed positions; the ि matra is written *before* its consonant even though it is read after.

Paragraph structure in Hindi mirrors English: indent or skip a line for new paragraphs; sentences end with the danda (।). For questions use the Hindi prashna chinha (?) — looks identical to the English one. Quotations use "..." in modern usage. Hindi does *not* use the sentence-final period (.) — that is reserved for abbreviations and decimals.

For an informal letter, open with प्रिय (dear) + name + comma; close with तुम्हारा / आपका (yours, m) — तुम्हारी / आपकी (yours, f) + your name. Formal letters use आदरणीय / श्रीमान् / श्रीमती + last name and end with सादर (sincerely).

## Common Mistakes

- Drawing the shirorekha first — it should be the last stroke connecting completed letters.
- Forgetting the danda at the end of sentences.
- Putting a matra on the wrong side: ि goes left, ी goes right — they look almost identical but flip direction.

## Try It Yourself

1. Write your name and address in Hindi by hand.
2. Compose a 4-sentence paragraph about your day.
3. Write a short note to a friend using तुम and one to your teacher using आप.
4. Practice forming each conjunct क्ष, त्र, ज्ञ, श्र five times.

- **प्रेमचंद की कहानियाँ गाँव के जीवन को दिखाती हैं।** (premcand kī kahāniyā̃ gā̃v ke jīvan ko dikhātī hai͂) — Premchand's stories depict village life.
- **"मधुशाला" हरिवंश राय बच्चन की प्रसिद्ध कविता है।** (madhuśālā harivanśa rāy baccan kī prasiddh kavitā hai) — "Madhushala" is Harivansh Rai Bachchan's famous poem.
- **गोदान एक प्रसिद्ध उपन्यास है।** (godān ek prasiddh upanyās hai) — *Godaan* is a famous novel.
- **उसने सच कहा।** (usne sac kahā) — He/she spoke the truth.
- **हमें न्याय चाहिए।** (hame͂ nyāy cāhie) — We need justice.

## Grammar / Script Notes

Literary Hindi leans heavily Sanskrit. Where colloquial Hindi says आदमी, literature says व्यक्ति or पुरुष; where speech says ज़िंदगी, books say जीवन. Recognizing the Sanskrit doublet of an Urdu-origin everyday word doubles your reading vocabulary fast.

Premchand's prose mixes Sanskrit terms with rural Avadhi/Bhojpuri texture; Bachchan's poetry uses Brajbhasha rhythm. Modern writers like Mahadevi Verma, Nirmal Verma, and Krishna Sobti pull more deeply from Sanskrit (Mahadevi) or use spare contemporary Hindi (Nirmal). When you pick up an excerpt, identify the register first — it tells you what verbs and lexicon to expect.

The perfective past (covered later) dominates narrative Hindi: उसने कहा (he said), वह गया (he went). Storytelling also uses the historical present — a present-tense verb where English would use past — for vividness. Watching for these patterns will speed your literary reading.

## Common Mistakes

- Translating प्रेम as "love" only — in literature it can be devotional, romantic, or filial; context decides.
- Skipping verses where word order is poetic-inverted — Hindi poetry uses Sanskrit-style flexible order.
- Treating व्यक्ति, इंसान, आदमी as interchangeable — they tag different registers.

| हरियाणवी | hariyāṇvī | Haryanvi |
| मैथिली | maithilī | Maithili |
| राजस्थानी | rājasthānī | Rajasthani |
| उच्चारण | uccāraṇ | pronunciation |
| शब्दावली | śabdāvalī | vocabulary |
| व्याकरण | vyākaraṇ | grammar |
| लिपि | lipi | script |
| देवनागरी | devnāgrī | Devanagari |
| नस्तालीक़ | nastālīq | Nastaliq (Urdu script) |
| मानक | mānak | standard |
| क्षेत्र | kṣetra | region |
| उपमहाद्वीप | upmahādvīp | subcontinent |

## Example Sentences

- **वह भोजपुरी बोलती है, हिन्दी नहीं।** (vah bhojpurī boltī hai, hindī nahī͂) — She speaks Bhojpuri, not Hindi.
- **उर्दू और हिन्दी की बोलचाल लगभग एक जैसी है।** (urdū aur hindī kī bolcāl lagbhag ek jaisī hai) — Spoken Urdu and Hindi are almost the same.
- **दिल्ली में हिंग्लिश आम है।** (dillī me͂ hiṅgliś ām hai) — Hinglish is common in Delhi.
- **मेरा गाँव अवधी क्षेत्र में है।** (merā gā̃v avadhī kṣetra me͂ hai) — My village is in the Awadhi region.
- **लिपि अलग है पर भाषा एक है।** (lipi alag hai par bhāṣā ek hai) — The script differs but the language is one.

## Grammar / Script Notes

Khari Boli (the standard taught in schools and used on TV) emerged around Delhi in the 19th century and became the basis for both modern Hindi and modern Urdu. The split is largely lexical and graphic: Hindi pulls vocabulary from Sanskrit and writes in Devanagari; Urdu pulls from Persian/Arabic and writes in Nastaliq. Spoken everyday speech in Delhi, Lucknow, and Karachi is mutually intelligible — bus conductors, shopkeepers, and taxi drivers do not pick a lane.

Bhojpuri (Bihar/east UP), Awadhi (central UP), Braj (around Mathura), Haryanvi (Haryana), and Rajasthani are *separate languages* by the linguistic measure of mutual intelligibility, but politically and educationally folded under "Hindi". Their grammar differs (verb endings, pronouns), so a Hindi learner won't automatically understand a Bhojpuri film without effort.

Hinglish is not a corruption — it's a stable register. "मुझे तुम्हारी हेल्प चाहिए" (I need your help), "वो थोड़ा अजीब था, but it was OK" — the matrix is Hindi grammar with English vocabulary inserts. Urban speakers, especially those educated in English, use it constantly.

## Common Mistakes

- Telling a Bhojpuri speaker their language is "broken Hindi" — it isn't, it's a separate language.
- Mixing Sanskrit-heavy Hindi with Urdu-heavy speech in the same sentence and clashing the register.
- Calling all Devanagari "Sanskrit script" — Devanagari is used by Hindi, Marathi, Nepali, Sanskrit, and others.

## Try It Yourself

1. Listen to one minute of Bhojpuri music and one of standard Hindi news; note three differences.
2. Find a tweet in Hinglish; rewrite it in pure Hindi.
3. Identify 5 Urdu-origin words you already use without thinking (बाज़ार, क़ीमत, ज़रूर, ख़ुश, तस्वीर).
4. Ask: "Which dialect is spoken where I am visiting?" and find out.

## Next Steps

The cultural unit gave you context. Now we extend grammar to past and future tenses.

# Past & Future Tenses

Hindi distinguishes simple past (perfective) from past habitual and past continuous, and uses ने ergative marking for transitive perfectives — a feature without an English parallel.

## Core Vocabulary

| Devanagari | Romanization | English |
|------------|--------------|---------|
| गया / गई / गए | gayā / gaī / gae | went (m / f / pl) |
| आया / आई / आए | āyā / āī / āe | came |
| किया / की / किए | kiyā / kī / kie | did |
| देखा / देखी / देखे | dekhā / dekhī / dekhe | saw |
| खाया | khāyā | ate |
| पिया | piyā | drank |
| बोला | bolā | spoke |
| था / थी / थे | thā / thī / the | was / were |
| जाएगा / जाएगी / जाएँगे | jāegā / jāegī / jāẽge | will go (m / f / pl) |
| करेगा | karegā | will do |
| होगा | hogā | will be |
| ने | ne | ergative marker |
| कल | kal | yesterday / tomorrow |
| परसों | parso͂ | day before / day after |
| अभी-अभी | abhī-abhī | just now |
| अगले हफ़्ते | agle hafte | next week |
| पिछले साल | pichle sāl | last year |
| जब | jab | when |
| बाद में | bād me͂ | later |
| पहले | pahle | before / earlier |

## Example Sentences

- **मैं कल बाज़ार गया।** (mai͂ kal bāzār gayā) — I went to the market yesterday. (m, intransitive — no ने)
- **उसने एक किताब पढ़ी।** (usne ek kitāb paṛhī) — He/she read a book. (transitive — ने appears, verb agrees with किताब, fem.)
- **राम ने रोटी खाई।** (rām ne roṭī khāī) — Ram ate bread. (transitive + ने)
- **हम पार्क में खेल रहे थे।** (ham pārk me͂ khel rahe the) — We were playing in the park.
- **मैं हर रोज़ स्कूल जाता था।** (mai͂ har roz skūl jātā thā) — I used to go to school every day.
- **कल बारिश होगी।** (kal bāriś hogī) — It will rain tomorrow.
- **मैं तुम्हारी मदद करूँगा।** (mai͂ tumhārī madad karū̃gā) — I will help you. (m speaker)

## Grammar / Script Notes

Hindi's most famous quirk: in **perfective transitive sentences**, the subject takes the postposition ने and the verb agrees with the *direct object*, not the subject. So राम ने किताब पढ़ी — verb पढ़ी agrees with feminine किताब, not with masculine राम. With intransitive verbs (जाना, आना, सोना), no ने and the verb agrees with the subject as usual.

A handful of verbs (बोलना, लाना, समझना, भूलना) are transitive but ne-less by tradition: मैं भूल गया (I forgot), not *मैंने भूल गया*. Memorize the exceptions.

**Future tense**: stem + ऊँगा/ऊँगी/एगा/एगी/एँगे/ओगे etc. The ending agrees with subject's gender and number. From करना: मैं करूँगा/करूँगी, तू करेगा, तुम करोगे, वह करेगा/करेगी, हम करेंगे, आप करेंगे, वे करेंगे.

The past auxiliary था/थी/थे inflects for gender and number: था (m sg), थी (f sg), थे (m pl/honorific), थीं (f pl). Past continuous = root + रहा था / रही थी / रहे थे. Past habitual = -ता + था / थी / थे.

## Common Mistakes

- Forgetting ने: *राम किताब पढ़ी* — should be राम ने किताब पढ़ी.
- Making the verb agree with the subject in ने sentences: *उसने किताब पढ़ा* — should be पढ़ी.
- Using ने with intransitive verbs: *मैंने गया* is wrong; *मैं गया* is correct.

## Try It Yourself

1. Conjugate देखना in past tense for मैं (m), मैंने, राम ने, सीता ने, हम ने.
2. Make 3 future tense sentences about your weekend.
3. Convert: मैं रोज़ चाय पीता हूँ → past habitual.
4. Translate: "Yesterday she ate a mango." (mind the ने and the agreement!)

## Next Steps

Hindi has a powerful compound verb system — that's next.

# Compound Verbs & Auxiliary Structures

Hindi loves compound verbs: a main verb stem + a helping verb (vector/light verb) that adds aspect, completion, intention, or social colour. They're a defining feature of fluent speech.

## Core Vocabulary

| Devanagari | Romanization | English |
|------------|--------------|---------|
| जाना | jānā | to go (also: completion vector) |
| लेना | lenā | to take (vector: for self / completion) |
| देना | denā | to give (vector: for someone else) |
| आना | ānā | to come (vector: starting / coming about) |
| डालना | ḍālnā | to drop / dump (vector: forceful / sudden) |
| उठना | uṭhnā | to rise (vector: sudden onset) |
| बैठना | baiṭhnā | to sit (vector: settling, often with regret) |
| रखना | rakhnā | to keep (vector: state achieved & maintained) |
| देखना | dekhnā | to see (vector: try / attempt) |
| पाना | pānā | to obtain / be able |
| सकना | saknā | can / be able |
| चाहिए | cāhie | should / ought |
| चाहना | cāhnā | to want |
| लगना | lagnā | to begin / seem |
| रहना | rahnā | to keep on / continue |
| होना | honā | to be / become |
| गिर जाना | gir jānā | to fall (down, completion) |
| खा लेना | khā lenā | to eat up (for oneself) |
| खा डालना | khā ḍālnā | to devour |
| बोल उठना | bol uṭhnā | to suddenly speak up |

## Example Sentences

- **वह गिर गया।** (vah gir gayā) — He fell. (gir + jānā = completion / unintentional)
- **मैंने सब खाना खा लिया।** (mai͂ne sab khānā khā liyā) — I ate up all the food. (खा + लेना = for myself, completion)
- **उसने मुझे पैसा दे दिया।** (usne mujhe paisā de diyā) — He gave me the money. (दे + देना = for the recipient, completion)
- **वह अचानक बोल उठा।** (vah acānak bol uṭhā) — He suddenly spoke up.
- **बच्चा रोने लगा।** (baccā rone lagā) — The child started to cry. (oblique infinitive + लगना = begin)
- **मुझे जाना चाहिए।** (mujhe jānā cāhie) — I should go. (infinitive + चाहिए)
- **मैं हिन्दी बोल सकता हूँ।** (mai͂ hindī bol saktā hū̃) — I can speak Hindi. (root + सकना)

## Grammar / Script Notes

The pattern is **main verb stem + light verb**, where the light verb conjugates and the main verb is bare: खा लेना → खा लिया, खा लेगा, खा लेता है. Choose the light verb for nuance:

- **लेना** (take): the action benefits the doer — खरीद लेना (buy for oneself), खा लेना (eat up).
- **देना** (give): the action benefits someone else — खरीद देना (buy for someone), लिख देना (write something for them).
- **जाना** (go): completion, often unintentional — मर जाना (to die / die-go), टूट जाना (to break-go).
- **उठना** (rise): sudden, surprised — रो उठना (burst into tears), बोल उठना (suddenly speak).
- **बैठना** (sit): often regretful — कह बैठना (blurt out unwisely), कर बैठना (do something rash).
- **डालना** (dump): forceful, decisive — फाड़ डालना (rip apart), मार डालना (kill outright).

**Modal-like structures** stack onto the main verb in different ways: रोना + लगा (started crying — oblique infinitive); जाना + चाहिए (should go — infinitive + invariable चाहिए); बोल + सकना (can speak — root + सकना). Each takes a different morphological slot.

## Common Mistakes

- Using लेना and देना randomly — *मैंने उसे पैसा खरीद लिया* sounds wrong; use खरीद दिया (bought for him).
- Adding जाना to every verb: *वह जा गया* is wrong; जाना itself is the verb, no compound needed for "he went" (वह गया).
- Mistaking लगना (begin) with लगना (seem): मुझे अच्छा लगता है (it seems good to me) is a sensation, not a beginning.

## Try It Yourself

1. Rewrite without compound, then add जाना: मैं सो + ___ → मैं सो गया.
2. Choose लेना vs देना: I bought a book *for myself* / *for my brother*.
3. Translate using a compound: "She suddenly laughed." / "I should sleep now."
4. Make 5 sentences using a different light verb each.

## Next Steps

Compounds give expressiveness; relative clauses give complexity. Next.

# Relative Clauses & Complex Sentences

Hindi uses **paired correlatives** — जो / वह, जब / तब, जहाँ / वहाँ, जैसा / वैसा — to glue clauses together. The "j" word introduces, the "v" word resolves.

## Core Vocabulary

| Devanagari | Romanization | English |
|------------|--------------|---------|
| जो | jo | who / which / that (relative) |
| वह | vah | he / she / it / that (correlative) |
| जब | jab | when (relative) |
| तब | tab | then |
| जहाँ | jahā̃ | where (relative) |
| वहाँ | vahā̃ | there |
| जैसा | jaisā | as / like (relative) |
| वैसा | vaisā | so / like that |
| जितना | jitnā | as much as (relative) |
| उतना | utnā | that much |
| क्योंकि | kyo͂ki | because |
| इसलिए | islie | therefore / so |
| अगर / यदि | agar / yadi | if |
| तो | to | then |
| लेकिन / पर | lekin / par | but |
| और | aur | and |
| या | yā | or |
| के बावजूद | ke bāvjūd | despite |
| ताकि | tāki | so that / in order that |
| वरना | varnā | otherwise |

## Example Sentences

- **जो लड़का वहाँ है, वह मेरा भाई है।** (jo laṛkā vahā̃ hai, vah merā bhāī hai) — The boy who is there is my brother.
- **जब मैं छोटा था, तब मैं गाँव में रहता था।** (jab mai͂ choṭā thā, tab mai͂ gā̃v me͂ rahtā thā) — When I was little, I lived in the village.
- **जहाँ तुम जाओगे, वहाँ मैं भी आऊँगी।** (jahā̃ tum jāoge, vahā̃ mai͂ bhī āū̃gī) — Wherever you go, I will come too.
- **अगर बारिश हुई तो हम घर रहेंगे।** (agar bāriś huī to ham ghar rahe͂ge) — If it rains, then we'll stay home.
- **वह नहीं आया क्योंकि वह बीमार था।** (vah nahī͂ āyā kyo͂ki vah bīmār thā) — He didn't come because he was sick.
- **मैं जल्दी निकला ताकि मैं समय पर पहुँचूँ।** (mai͂ jaldī niklā tāki mai͂ samay par pahu͂cū̃) — I left early so that I'd arrive on time.

## Grammar / Script Notes

The defining feature of Hindi relative clauses is the **correlative pair**: the relative clause comes first with जो/जब/जहाँ, and the main clause follows with वह/तब/वहाँ "resolving" the reference. Both halves are usually full clauses: जो आदमी कल आया था, वह डॉक्टर है (The man who came yesterday — *that* one — is a doctor).

The relative clause can come *before* the main clause (most common) or after, but if it comes after, the correlative in the main clause becomes optional and the order resembles English: मैं उस आदमी को जानता हूँ जो कल आया था (I know the man who came yesterday).

जो inflects for case (के बारे में जो... → जिसके बारे में, "about whom") in oblique contexts: जिसने (who, ne-form), जिसको (whom), जिसमें (in which), जिनसे (from whom, plural). Same for जब → जब-जब, जहाँ → जहाँ-जहाँ for emphasis.

**Conditional sentences**: अगर/यदि + clause + तो + result. Past counterfactual ("if X had happened, Y would have...") uses the perfective participle: अगर वह आता तो हम जाते (If he came/were to come, we would go) — same form for present and past hypothetical.

## Common Mistakes

- Dropping the correlative: *जो लड़का आया, मेरा भाई है* — needs वह for fluency: जो लड़का आया, वह मेरा भाई है.
- Translating "if ... then" without तो: native Hindi almost always pairs अगर/यदि with तो.
- Confusing क्योंकि (because, supports a clause) with के कारण (due to, takes a noun): वह नहीं आया, बारिश के कारण.

## Try It Yourself

1. Rewrite as a relative clause: "I read the book. The book is interesting."
2. Make a conditional: "If you study, then you will pass."
3. Use जब / तब to describe a memory.
4. Use ताकि to express purpose: "I'm learning Hindi so that I can travel in India."

## Next Steps

We close the course with formal Hindi, idioms, and exam prep.

# Formal Hindi & Administrative Language

Government Hindi (राजभाषा हिंदी) is heavy with Sanskrit-origin (तत्सम) words and Persian-origin officialese. It's the register of forms, court orders, news anchors, and academic writing.

## Core Vocabulary

| Devanagari | Romanization | English |
|------------|--------------|---------|
| आवेदन | āvedan | application |
| आवेदक | āvedak | applicant |
| आदेश | ādeś | order |
| अधिनियम | adhiniyam | act / statute |
| नियम | niyam | rule |
| उपबंध | upbandh | provision |
| सूचना | sūcnā | notice / information |
| प्रकाशन | prakāśan | publication |
| प्रशासन | praśāsan | administration |
| कार्यालय | kāryālay | office (formal) |
| विभाग | vibhāg | department |
| मंत्रालय | mantrālay | ministry |
| कर्मचारी | karmcārī | employee |
| अधिकारी | adhikārī | officer |
| हस्ताक्षर | hastākṣar | signature |
| दिनांक | dinā̃k | date (formal) |
| संदर्भ | sandarbh | reference / context |
| उपर्युक्त | uparyukt | above-mentioned |
| निवेदन | nivedan | humble request |
| सादर | sādar | sincerely / with respect |
| भवदीय | bhavdīy | yours sincerely |

## Example Sentences

- **उपर्युक्त संदर्भ में हम सूचित करते हैं कि...** (uparyukt sandarbh me͂ ham sūcit karte hai͂ ki...) — In reference to the above, we inform that...
- **कृपया दिनांक 1 अप्रैल तक आवेदन प्रस्तुत करें।** (kṛpayā dinā̃k 1 aprail tak āvedan prastut kare͂) — Please submit the application by 1 April.
- **यह आदेश तुरंत प्रभाव से लागू होगा।** (yah ādeś turant prabhāv se lāgū hogā) — This order will be in effect immediately.
- **मंत्रालय ने नया नियम जारी किया।** (mantrālay ne nayā niyam jārī kiyā) — The ministry has issued a new rule.
- **भवदीय,** (bhavdīy) — Yours sincerely, (formal letter sign-off)

## Grammar / Script Notes

Formal Hindi prefers **passive constructions** and **noun-heavy phrasing**: instead of "we received the application", you'll see आवेदन प्राप्त किया गया (the application was received). The agent is often suppressed entirely. Verbs cluster at the end, sometimes with multiple auxiliary stacks: किया जाना है, की जा सकती है.

Word choice swings Sanskrit-ward: speech-level काम becomes कार्य; घर becomes आवास; देखना becomes अवलोकन / निरीक्षण करना; पैसा becomes मुद्रा / धन / राशि. Reading a government circular is largely a vocabulary problem, not a grammar one.

Formal letters follow templates. Headings: **विषय** (subject), **संदर्भ** (reference), **दिनांक** (date), **प्रति** (to). Body uses महोदय/महोदया (Sir/Madam), then numbered paragraphs. Closings: सादर / भवदीय / आपका विश्वासी (yours faithfully).

Numbers and dates are written in formal style: दिनांक 5 जून 2026 or दिनांक 5/6/2026; sometimes the Saka era (शक संवत्) appears alongside Gregorian. Times use 24-hour format and बजे (o'clock) — 14 बजे = 2 PM.

## Common Mistakes

- Using colloquial verbs in formal text: *पैसा भेजना* in a letter — say राशि भेजना or राशि प्रेषित करना.
- Using तुम / तू forms — formal Hindi is आप only, often dropped entirely in favor of passive.
- Forgetting विषय (subject line) — administrative letters are unreadable without it.

## Try It Yourself

1. Write a one-paragraph formal request to a government office.
2. Convert: "I want to apply for a passport" into formal Hindi.
3. Identify Sanskrit-origin doublets for: काम, घर, पैसा, देखना.
4. Read a Hindi government notice (rajbhasha.gov.in) and list 10 formal terms.

## Next Steps

Formal Hindi tightens you up. Idioms loosen you back up.

# Idioms, Proverbs & Slang

Hindi muhavare (idioms) and lokoktiyan (proverbs) are dense with imagery — body parts, animals, weather, kitchen items. Slang shifts fast in the cities.

## Core Vocabulary

| Devanagari | Romanization | English |
|------------|--------------|---------|
| मुहावरा | muhāvarā | idiom |
| लोकोक्ति / कहावत | lokokti / kahāvat | proverb / saying |
| आँख का तारा | ā̃kh kā tārā | apple of one's eye (lit. "star of the eye") |
| नाक में दम करना | nāk me͂ dam karnā | to harass (lit. "put life in the nose") |
| दिल खोलकर | dil kholkar | wholeheartedly |
| सिर पर चढ़ना | sir par caṛhnā | to be spoiled / get cocky |
| हाथ धो बैठना | hāth dho baiṭhnā | to lose hope |

## Example Sentences

- **तुम मेरी आँख का तारा हो।** (tum merī ā̃kh kā tārā ho) — You are the apple of my eye.
- **उसने मेरी नाक में दम कर दिया।** (usne merī nāk me͂ dam kar diyā) — He drove me crazy.
- **यह मदद ऊँट के मुँह में जीरा है।** (yah madad ū̃ṭ ke mu̇̃h me͂ jīrā hai) — This help is a drop in the ocean.
- **यार, क्या बकवास है!** (yār, kyā bakvās hai!) — Dude, what nonsense!
- **जुगाड़ लगा लो।** (jugāṛ lagā lo) — Improvise / find a workaround.
- **टाइमपास के लिए फ़िल्म देख रहे हैं।** (ṭāimpās ke lie film dekh rahe hai͂) — We're watching a movie for timepass.

## Grammar / Script Notes

Idioms freeze archaic grammar — the verb often cannot be conjugated freely. आँख का तारा (apple of the eye) survives as a noun phrase; you cannot say *आँख का चाँद* (moon of the eye) and expect to be understood. Treat each idiom as a memorized unit.

Many proverbs have an A-B parallel structure: जैसा X वैसा Y (as X, so Y), X-गए Y-गए (rhyming pairs), or twin-clause comparisons: ऊँचा बोल नहीं तो रोल नहीं. The rhythm is part of the meaning — and the reason they stick.

Slang is heavily Mumbai-, Delhi-, or college-flavored. यार is universal; झकास is Mumbai (popularized by Anil Kapoor); फ़ंडा and स्कीम and चिल are urban-college; बहुत हार्ड है from regional Punjabi-influenced YouTube. New slang turns over yearly.

Many "Hindi" idioms are Urdu-Persian inheritance: हाथ-पाँव मारना (try hard), ख़ाक छानना (search desperately, "to sift dust"), दिल बाग़-बाग़ होना (heart blooms). Their vocabulary tags Persian origin (ख़ाक, दिल, बाग़).

## Common Mistakes

- Translating idioms word-for-word into Hindi from English — they almost never map. "Break a leg" is not *पैर तोड़ो*.
- Using slang in formal contexts — यार in a job interview is a no-go.
- Treating proverbs as advice in modern conversation — many sound dated. Use sparingly.

## Try It Yourself

1. Memorize 5 idioms; use each in a sentence.
2. Find an English idiom and a Hindi idiom with the *same meaning* — note how the imagery differs.
3. Listen to a Hindi stand-up clip; flag 3 slang terms and look them up.
4. Write a 5-line exchange between two friends using at least 3 slang words.

## Next Steps

The main standardized test is the **Hindi Pravinya / Praveen / Visharad** sequence (Wardha) and the Indian government's **CHTET / Hindi Sevak / OCI Hindi proficiency** rubrics. ## Example Sentences

- **अगले महीने मेरी हिंदी परीक्षा है।** (agle mahīne merī hindī parīkṣā hai) — My Hindi exam is next month.
- **मुझे व्याकरण और निबंध दोनों में अभ्यास चाहिए।** (mujhe vyākaraṇ aur nibandh dono͂ me͂ abhyās cāhie) — I need practice in both grammar and essay.
- **समय सीमा का ध्यान रखें।** (samay sīmā kā dhyān rakhe͂) — Mind the time limit.
- **यह प्रश्न बहुविकल्पीय है।** (yah praśn bahuvikalpīy hai) — This question is multiple-choice.
- **दो सौ शब्दों में सारांश लिखिए।** (do sau śabdo͂ me͂ sārāṅś likhie) — Write a summary in 200 words.

## Grammar / Script Notes

Most Hindi proficiency exams sample five skills: **listening** (श्रवण), **reading** (पठन), **writing** (लेखन — essay + summary + letter), **grammar** (व्याकरण), and sometimes **translation** (अनुवाद) or **speaking** (भाषण). Question types include multiple-choice (बहुविकल्पीय), fill-in-the-blanks (रिक्त स्थान भरें), match-the-pairs (मिलान करें), and short-answer (संक्षिप्त उत्तर).

For the **essay** section, plan a 250–500 word piece around an introduction (परिचय), three body paragraphs (विकास), and a conclusion (निष्कर्ष). Use clear topic sentences and connectors like इसके अतिरिक्त (additionally), इसके विपरीत (in contrast), अंत में (finally), निष्कर्षतः (in conclusion).

For **summary** (सारांश), aim for one-third of the original length, retaining all key points and the original tone. Use the third person and avoid copy-pasting whole sentences. Wardha exams also expect the candidate to produce a title for the summary.

For **grammar**, the high-yield areas are: ने ergative usage, gender agreement of compound subjects, postposition + oblique, perfective participle agreement, conditional structures, and conjunct verbs. Memorize 20 idioms — they appear regularly.

For **listening**, slow down only after you've identified the speaker's main argument; details (numbers, dates) are easier to flag the second pass. For **reading**, scan headings and topic sentences first.

## Common Mistakes

- Writing an essay without a thesis — examiners reward structure.
- Translating idioms literally — pick equivalents in the target language.
- Spending equal time on each section — allocate by mark value.

## Try It Yourself

1. Plan a 250-word essay outline on "मेरा आदर्श" (My ideal).
2. Summarize a Hindi news article (300 words) into 100 words.
3. Take a 30-minute timed grammar quiz with 25 questions.
4. Record yourself speaking for 2 minutes about your weekend in Hindi; review for tense agreement.

## Next Steps

Beyond exams, the real goal is fluency — so keep reading Premchand, watching OTT, talking with friends. हिन्दी सीखना एक यात्रा है, मंज़िल नहीं। (Learning Hindi is a journey, not a destination.)
